clinicalPearls: Diffuse peripatellar or retropatellar pain aggravated by activities that load the flexed knee, such as stairs, squatting and running
Pain after prolonged sitting with the knee bent (the theatre sign) is characteristic
It is one of the commonest causes of knee pain in active adolescents and young adults, especially women
Contributing factors include abnormal patellar tracking, muscle imbalance, weakness of the hip and quadriceps, and training overload
It is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging is used mainly to exclude other pathology
Structured physiotherapy focusing on hip and quadriceps strength and load management is the mainstay of treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Patellofemoral pain syndrome is a multifactorial overuse condition in which altered load distribution across the patellofemoral joint irritates pain-sensitive structures. Malalignment or maltracking of the patella, weakness or imbalance of the quadriceps and hip abductors and external rotators, and excessive or rapidly increased loading all contribute to abnormal patellofemoral stress. The pain arises from the richly innervated subchondral bone, synovium and peripatellar soft tissues rather than from cartilage, which is aneural.
additionalDifferentials: Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of pain reproduction and patellar tracking
Evaluation of hip and quadriceps strength and lower-limb biomechanics
Radiographs if structural abnormality, instability or arthritis is suspected
MRI reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected internal derangement
Assessment of training load and footwear
redFlags: True locking or giving way suggesting internal derangement or instability
Night pain or systemic features suggesting other pathology
Focal tendon or bony tenderness pointing to an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with a sustained rehabilitation programme, though symptoms can be persistent or recurrent, particularly if underlying strength and biomechanical factors are not addressed.
pitfalls: Over-investigating with imaging for a clinical diagnosis
Neglecting hip and proximal muscle strengthening
Missing patellar instability or internal derangement
Advising rest alone rather than active rehabilitation
management: Deliver a sustained rehabilitation programme centred on hip abductor and external-rotator and quadriceps strengthening as the primary treatment
Apply load management, reducing activities that stress the flexed knee while maintaining conditioning
Add patellar taping or bracing and foot orthoses as short-term adjuncts to support pain relief and exercise
Retrain running and landing mechanics and correct training-load errors and footwear
Use imaging and specialist referral selectively, mainly to exclude other pathology in refractory or atypical presentations
Provide education and reassurance to encourage adherence, as symptoms often persist without correction of strength and biomechanical deficits
